items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The list of successful candidates ______ been put up on the notice board.

steps: The subject is 'list' (singular); 'of successful candidates' only describes it. So the verb is 'has been put up'.
Completed sentence: *The list of successful candidates has been put up on the notice board.*
solution.trap: 'candidates' is closest to the blank and pulls you towards 'have'.
solution.rule: The verb agrees with the head noun, not with the noun inside an 'of' phrase

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

She waited for ______ hour at the bus stop before the bus finally came.

steps: 'hour' begins with a silent 'h', so it starts with a vowel sound and takes 'an'. 'few', 'many' and 'much' cannot go before a singular countable noun.
Completed sentence: *She waited for an hour at the bus stop before the bus finally came.*
solution.trap: The letter 'h' looks like a consonant, but the article follows the sound.
solution.rule: Articles: 'an' before a vowel sound (an hour, an honest man)

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The meeting will begin ______ 10 a.m. sharp.

steps: An exact clock time takes 'at' (at 10 a.m.); 'on' is for days and dates, 'in' for months, years and parts of the day.
Completed sentence: *The meeting will begin at 10 a.m. sharp.*
solution.trap: 'since' needs a perfect tense and a starting point; it cannot follow 'will begin'.
solution.rule: Prepositions of time: at + clock time, on + day/date, in + month/year

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Look! The children ______ in the rain.

steps: 'Look!' shows that the action is happening right now, so the present continuous 'are playing' is needed.
Completed sentence: *Look! The children are playing in the rain.*
solution.trap: 'play' is the simple present, used for habits, not for something happening now.
solution.rule: Present continuous for an action happening at the moment of speaking

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Between you and ______, the plan is unlikely to work.

steps: 'Between' is a preposition, and a pronoun after a preposition takes the object form: 'between you and me'.
Completed sentence: *Between you and me, the plan is unlikely to work.*
solution.trap: 'between you and I' sounds polite but is an error.
solution.rule: Pronouns: object form after a preposition

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Of all the students in the class, Ravi is the ______.

steps: 'Of all the students' compares Ravi with more than two people, so the superlative 'tallest' is needed.
Completed sentence: *Of all the students in the class, Ravi is the tallest.*
solution.trap: 'most tallest' is a double superlative; 'tall' already takes -est.
solution.rule: Superlative for comparing one with three or more

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

My grandmother enjoys ______ old Hindi songs on the radio.

steps: 'enjoy' is always followed by a gerund (-ing form): 'enjoys listening to'.
Completed sentence: *My grandmother enjoys listening to old Hindi songs on the radio.*
solution.trap: 'enjoys to listen' is a common error; 'enjoy' never takes a to-infinitive.
solution.rule: Gerund after verbs like enjoy, avoid, finish, mind

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

She can speak Tamil, ______?

steps: A positive statement takes a negative tag, and the tag repeats the helping verb 'can': 'can't she?'.
Completed sentence: *She can speak Tamil, can't she?*
solution.trap: 'doesn't she' would need a sentence without a helping verb, like 'She speaks Tamil'.
solution.rule: Question tags: positive statement → negative tag with the same helping verb

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

One of my friends ______ a new bicycle.

steps: The subject is 'One' (of my friends), which is singular, so the verb is singular: 'has bought'.
Completed sentence: *One of my friends has bought a new bicycle.*
solution.trap: 'friends' is next to the verb, but it is not the subject.
solution.rule: 'One of the + plural noun' takes a singular verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Each of the boys has brought his lunch.
Each of the boys have brought their lunch.
Neither of the girls were ready for the test.
Every student and teacher were present.
The box of apples are on the table.

steps: 'Each of the boys has' is correct: 'each' is singular.
The others need 'has', 'was', 'was' and 'is': 'neither of', 'every … and every …' and 'The box' are all singular subjects.
solution.trap: A plural noun after 'of' does not make the subject plural.
solution.rule: Each, every, either, neither → singular verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: If you heat water to 100 degrees Celsius, it boils.
If I see her, I will give her the message.
If it will rain tomorrow, we will stay at home.
If he had studied, he would have passed.

steps: 'If it will rain' is wrong: in a first conditional the 'if' clause takes the simple present: 'If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home'.
The other three are correct zero, first and third conditionals.
solution.trap: 'tomorrow' tempts you to put 'will' in both clauses.
solution.rule: First conditional: If + simple present, will + verb

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

She sings very ______.

steps: The blank describes how she sings (the verb), so an adverb is needed: 'sweetly'.
Completed sentence: *She sings very sweetly.*
solution.trap: 'sweet' is an adjective; it describes a noun (a sweet voice), not a verb.
solution.rule: An adverb, not an adjective, describes an action verb

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

I ______ in this city since 2015.

steps: 'since 2015' marks an action that began in the past and is still going on, so the present perfect 'have lived' is needed.
Completed sentence: *I have lived in this city since 2015.*
solution.trap: 'am living since 2015' is a common Indian-English error.
solution.rule: Present perfect with 'since' / 'for' for an action continuing to the present

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

He is ______ European who has settled in Goa.

steps: 'European' begins with a 'yoo' sound, which is a consonant sound, so the article is 'a'.
Completed sentence: *He is a European who has settled in Goa.*
solution.trap: 'European' starts with the vowel letter 'E', but the sound is 'yoo'.
solution.rule: Articles: 'a' before a consonant sound (a European, a university, a one-rupee coin)

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The farmer died of cholera last year.
They discussed about the plan for hours.
We reached at the station late.

steps: 'die of' a disease is correct.
The others should be 'fond of music', 'prefers tea to coffee', 'discussed the plan' (no preposition) and 'reached the station' (no preposition).
solution.trap: 'discuss about' and 'reach at' add a preposition where none is needed.
solution.rule: Prepositions: fixed pairs (die of, fond of, prefer … to) and verbs that take no preposition (discuss, reach)

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Let you and I finish the work first.
The book is hers, not yours.
They blamed themselves for the delay.

steps: 'Let' is followed by the object form, so it should be 'Let you and me finish the work first'.
The other sentences use the pronouns correctly: 'She and I' as subject, 'hers' and 'yours' as possessives, 'themselves' as a reflexive.
solution.trap: Remove 'you and': 'Let I finish' is clearly wrong.
solution.rule: Pronouns: object form after 'let' and after prepositions

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: While walking to the office, a stray dog began following me.
Having finished the work, the lights were switched off.
Driving through the ghat, the valley looked beautiful.
While I was walking to the office, a stray dog began following me.
After eating lunch, the bus left for Ooty.

steps: Only the correct sentence has a full clause ('I was walking') with its own subject.
In the others the opening phrase attaches to the wrong subject: the dog was not walking to the office, the lights did not finish the work, the valley was not driving, and the bus did not eat lunch.
solution.trap: The first wrong option is almost identical to the right one; only the missing 'I was' separates them.
solution.rule: A participle phrase at the start must refer to the subject of the main clause

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

If I ______ you, I would apologise at once.

steps: An imaginary present situation ('If I … you') takes the second conditional: If + past (were for all persons), would + verb.
Completed sentence: *If I were you, I would apologise at once.*
solution.trap: 'had been' would need 'would have apologised'.
solution.rule: Second conditional: If + past (were), would + verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: She likes reading, to write and painting.
He is honest, hard-working and has intelligence.
The job requires patience, skill and to be honest.
We went there to relax, to eat and for shopping.
She likes reading, writing and painting.

steps: All three items in the correct sentence are gerunds.
The others mix forms: gerunds with an infinitive, adjectives with a verb phrase, nouns with an infinitive, and infinitives with a prepositional phrase.
solution.trap: Each wrong sentence breaks the pattern only in its last item.
solution.rule: Parallelism: items joined by 'and' must have the same grammatical form

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Nobody came to the party, ______?

steps: 'Nobody' makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive. Indefinite pronouns like 'nobody' are referred to by 'they': 'did they?'.
Completed sentence: *Nobody came to the party, did they?*
solution.trap: 'Nobody came' has no 'not', so it looks positive.
solution.rule: Question tags: negative words (nobody, never, hardly) take a positive tag; nobody / everybody → they

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

He is used to ______ late at night.

steps: In 'be used to' the word 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by a gerund: 'is used to working'.
Completed sentence: *He is used to working late at night.*
solution.trap: Do not confuse it with 'used to work' (a past habit).
solution.rule: be used to / look forward to / object to + -ing

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: He is more stronger than his brother.
This is the best film I have seen this year.
Mumbai is larger than any other city in Maharashtra.
She is senior to me by two years.

steps: 'more stronger' is a double comparative; it should be 'stronger'.
The other three are correct: a superlative, 'any other' within the same group, and 'senior to'.
solution.trap: 'senior to' looks odd but is correct; Latin comparatives take 'to'.
solution.rule: Do not use 'more' with a comparative already ending in -er

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Neither the manager nor his assistants ______ available on Saturday.

steps: With 'neither … nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'assistants' (plural), so the plural 'were' is the only correct form offered.
Completed sentence: *Neither the manager nor his assistants were available on Saturday.*
solution.trap: 'Neither' alone takes a singular verb, but 'neither … nor' follows the nearer noun.
solution.rule: Neither … nor / either … or: the verb agrees with the nearer subject

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

One of the lights in the corridor ______ out of order since Monday.

steps: The subject is 'One' (singular), and 'since Monday' needs the present perfect: 'has been out of order'.
Completed sentence: *One of the lights in the corridor has been out of order since Monday.*
solution.trap: 'have been' agrees with 'lights', which is not the subject.
solution.rule: 'One of the + plural noun' takes a singular verb; 'since' needs a perfect tense

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: By the time we reached the cinema, the film had started.
He did not came to the office yesterday.

steps: The correct sentence uses the past perfect for the earlier of two past actions.
The others should be 'I saw him yesterday', 'She knows the answer' (know is not used in the continuous), 'did not come', and 'have been living here since 2010'.
solution.trap: 'did not came' uses two past forms; after 'did' the base verb is used.
solution.rule: Tenses: past perfect for the earlier past action; no present perfect with a finished time

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

______ Ganga is considered a sacred river by millions of people.

steps: Names of rivers take the definite article: 'The Ganga', 'the Narmada'.
Completed sentence: *The Ganga is considered a sacred river by millions of people.*
solution.trap: Most proper names take no article, but rivers are an exception.
solution.rule: Articles: 'the' before names of rivers, seas, oceans and mountain ranges

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: He drives carefully on the highway.
She looks beautifully in that saree.

steps: 'look' here is a linking verb (it describes her appearance), so it takes an adjective: 'She looks beautiful'.
'tastes delicious' is also a linking verb with an adjective; 'drives carefully' and 'running late' are correct.
solution.trap: 'beautifully' sounds more formal, but linking verbs do not take adverbs.
solution.rule: Linking verbs (look, seem, taste, feel, smell) take adjectives

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The new rule will come ______ effect from 1 April.

steps: The fixed phrase is 'come into effect' (or 'come into force').
Completed sentence: *The new rule will come into effect from 1 April.*
solution.trap: 'come in effect' is a frequent slip.
solution.rule: Fixed phrase: come into effect / force

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: He hardly ever comes late, doesn't he?
They are going to Agra, isn't it?
There is a bank nearby, isn't it?
Let's go for a walk, shall we?

steps: After 'Let's' (a suggestion) the tag is 'shall we?'.
The others should be 'does he?' (hardly is negative), 'aren't they?', 'isn't there?' and 'can she?'.
solution.trap: 'isn't it?' is the all-purpose tag of spoken Indian English, but it is not correct in writing.
solution.rule: Question tags repeat the helping verb and the subject pronoun, with the opposite polarity

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Had I known about the sale, I ______ more books.

steps: 'Had I known' is an inverted third conditional (= If I had known), so the result is 'would have bought'.
Completed sentence: *Had I known about the sale, I would have bought more books.*
solution.trap: The missing 'if' hides that this is a conditional.
solution.rule: Third conditional: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The quality of the mangoes were not good.
Bread and butter is a common breakfast.
The jury has given its verdict.
Ten kilometres is a long distance to walk.

steps: The subject is 'quality' (singular), so it should be 'was not good'.
The others are correct: 'bread and butter' is one dish, the jury acts as one body, and a distance is one amount.
solution.trap: 'Bread and butter is' looks wrong but is correct.
solution.rule: The verb agrees with the head noun, not the noun in the 'of' phrase

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The committee has submitted ______ report to the board.

steps: 'The committee has' treats the committee as a single body, so the possessive is 'its'.
Completed sentence: *The committee has submitted its report to the board.*
solution.trap: 'it's' looks possessive because of the apostrophe.
solution.rule: Pronouns: 'its' is the possessive; 'it's' means 'it is'

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

She is one of those officers who ______ never late for work.

steps: 'who' refers to 'officers' (plural), not to 'one', so the verb in the relative clause is plural: 'who are never late'.
Completed sentence: *She is one of those officers who are never late for work.*
solution.trap: The singular rule for 'one of the …' applies to the main verb, not to the 'who' clause.
solution.rule: In 'one of those + plural noun + who …', the relative clause takes a plural verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Not only the students but also the teacher were surprised.
A pair of shoes were lying under the bed.
The number of accidents have gone down.
The captain, along with his players, was received at the airport.
Either you or he are responsible.

steps: 'along with his players' does not change the subject 'The captain', so 'was' is right.
The others need 'was' (the nearer subject 'teacher'), 'was' ('A pair'), 'has' ('The number') and 'is' (the nearer subject 'he').
solution.trap: 'the teacher were' fails because the verb follows the nearer subject in 'not only … but also'.
solution.rule: 'along with', 'as well as', 'together with' do not change the number of the subject

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

I ______ for two hours when the power finally came back.

steps: A continuing action with a duration ('for two hours') that ended at a past moment ('came back') takes the past perfect continuous.
Completed sentence: *I had been waiting for two hours when the power finally came back.*
solution.trap: 'have been waiting' measures up to now, but 'came back' fixes the time in the past.
solution.rule: Past perfect continuous: duration up to a point in the past

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The gold in this ring is of poor quality.
The gold is a precious metal.
He goes to church every Sunday.
The rich should help the poor.

steps: A material in general takes no article: 'Gold is a precious metal'.
'The gold in this ring' is correct because it is specific; 'go to church' (for worship) and 'the rich' (a class of people) are correct.
solution.trap: The first correct sentence also has 'The gold', but there it refers to particular gold.
solution.rule: Articles: no article for materials and abstract nouns used in a general sense

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The climate of Bengaluru is milder than ______ of Chennai.

steps: The comparison must be between climate and climate, so a singular pronoun standing for 'the climate' is needed: 'that of Chennai'.
Completed sentence: *The climate of Bengaluru is milder than that of Chennai.*
solution.trap: 'those' is plural and cannot replace 'climate'.
solution.rule: Compare like with like: 'that of' (singular), 'those of' (plural)

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: She avoided to meet him at the function.
They look forward to meet you.
I remember locking the door before I left.
He is capable to handle the pressure.
We are considering to shift to Pune.

steps: 'remember + -ing' refers to a memory of an earlier action, which fits 'before I left'.
The others need 'avoided meeting', 'look forward to meeting', 'capable of handling' and 'considering shifting'.
solution.trap: 'capable to' is a common slip; the adjective takes 'of' + -ing.
solution.rule: Gerund after avoid, consider, look forward to, capable of

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

If she had taken the job in Delhi last year, she ______ in a bigger flat now.

steps: This is a mixed conditional: an unreal past condition ('had taken … last year') with a present result ('now'), so 'would be living'.
Completed sentence: *If she had taken the job in Delhi last year, she would be living in a bigger flat now.*
solution.trap: 'would have lived' refers to the past and clashes with 'now'.
solution.rule: Mixed conditional: If + past perfect, would + verb (present result)

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The manager asked us to finish the report, check the figures and that we should send it by noon.
He was praised not only for his courage but also for his honesty.
She would rather walk than take the bus.
Either we leave now or we miss the train.

steps: The list after 'asked us' mixes infinitives with a 'that' clause; it should be 'to finish the report, check the figures and send it by noon'.
The other three keep matching forms after 'not only … but also', 'rather … than' and 'either … or'.
solution.trap: The error appears only in the last item of the list.
solution.rule: Parallelism: every item in a list must have the same form

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Having missed the last bus, an auto was our only option.
Being a holiday, the offices were closed.
On entering the hall, the lights went off.
Having missed the last bus, we had to take an auto.
Walking in the park, a snake frightened the children.

steps: 'we' missed the bus, so the opening phrase attaches correctly.
In the others the phrase dangles: an auto did not miss the bus, the offices were not a holiday, the lights did not enter the hall, and the snake was not walking in the park.
solution.trap: 'Being a holiday' needs 'It being a holiday' to be correct.
solution.rule: Dangling modifier: an opening phrase must describe the subject that follows it

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

I am late again, ______?

steps: The accepted negative tag for 'I am' is 'aren't I?'.
Completed sentence: *I am late again, aren't I?*
solution.trap: 'amn't I' seems logical but is not standard; 'am not I' has the wrong word order (it would be 'am I not?').
solution.rule: Question tags: 'I am …, aren't I?'

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: He has been absent since three days.
The house was built of stone.
We congratulated her on her success.

steps: 'three days' is a length of time, so it takes 'for': 'absent for three days'.
The others are correct: good at, built of, congratulate on.
solution.trap: The present perfect makes 'since' feel right, but the noun is a duration.
solution.rule: since + point of time; for + length of time

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The patient is doing ______ after the operation.

steps: 'doing' is an action verb, so the adverb 'well' is needed to describe how the patient is progressing.
Completed sentence: *The patient is doing well after the operation.*
solution.trap: 'doing good' is common in speech but is not correct for health.
solution.rule: 'well' is the adverb (and the adjective for health); 'good' is only an adjective

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The manager and I have been invited to the conference.
Me and my brother went to Agra.
This is between he and his wife.
Whom do you think is the best candidate?
The prize was shared by Ravi and I.

steps: 'The manager and I' is a subject, so the subject form 'I' is correct.
The others need 'My brother and I' (subject), 'between him and his wife' and 'by Ravi and me' (objects of prepositions), and 'Who … is' (subject of 'is').
solution.trap: 'Whom do you think is …' looks formal but 'who' is the subject of 'is'.
solution.rule: Subject pronouns (I, he, who) as subjects; object pronouns (me, him, whom) after verbs and prepositions

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Twenty thousand rupees ______ too much to pay for a phone like this.

steps: A sum of money treated as one amount takes a singular verb: 'Twenty thousand rupees is too much'.
Completed sentence: *Twenty thousand rupees is too much to pay for a phone like this.*
solution.trap: The plural noun 'rupees' pulls you towards 'are'.
solution.rule: Amounts of money, time and distance taken as a whole → singular verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: One of the windows is broken.
She is one of the students who have been selected for the camp.
Each one of the buses has a first-aid kit.
Neither of the answers is correct.

steps: All four sentences are correct.

'One of the windows is' and 'Each one of the buses has' take a singular verb; in 'one of the students who have been selected', 'who' refers to 'students', so the verb is plural; 'Neither of' takes a singular verb.
solution.trap: The second sentence looks like an agreement error, but it is correct.
solution.rule: 'One of the …' → singular main verb; 'one of the … who' → plural verb in the 'who' clause

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The minister refused ______ any questions about the project.

steps: 'refuse' is followed by a to-infinitive: 'refused to answer'.
Completed sentence: *The minister refused to answer any questions about the project.*
solution.trap: 'to answering' would need a verb like 'objected to', not 'refused'.
solution.rule: to-infinitive after refuse, decide, agree, promise, hope

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Had the bank raised its rates, borrowers would feel the pinch last year.
Should the bank will raise its rates, borrowers would feel the pinch.
If the bank would raise its rates, borrowers would have felt the pinch.
Were the bank to raise its rates, borrowers would feel the pinch.
Were the bank raised its rates, borrowers would feel the pinch.

steps: 'Were the bank to raise …, borrowers would feel …' is a correct inverted hypothetical (= If the bank were to raise).
The others fail: 'last year' needs 'would have felt'; 'Should … will raise' doubles the modal; 'If … would raise' puts 'would' in the if-clause; 'Were the bank raised its rates' mixes two verbs.
solution.trap: Each wrong option looks formal; check the tense of each clause.
solution.rule: Inverted conditionals: Were + subject + to-infinitive; Should + subject + base verb; Had + subject + past participle

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The committee's recommendations, along with the dissenting note, has been forwarded to the ministry.
Neither the chairman nor the directors were aware of the lapse.
What the bank needs now is patient capital.
A number of branches have been merged this year.

steps: The subject is 'recommendations' (plural); 'along with the dissenting note' does not change it, so 'have been forwarded'.
The others are correct: the nearer subject 'directors' → were; a 'What' clause → is; 'A number of' → plural.
solution.trap: 'note' is next to the verb and is singular, which makes 'has' sound right.
solution.rule: Phrases with 'along with' do not change the number of the subject

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Scarcely ______ the results when the website crashed.

steps: 'Scarcely' at the start forces inversion, and the earlier of the two past actions takes the past perfect: 'Scarcely had the board announced … when …'.
Completed sentence: *Scarcely had the board announced the results when the website crashed.*
solution.trap: 'did the board announce' inverts correctly but uses the wrong tense.
solution.rule: Scarcely / Hardly + had + subject + past participle … when + past

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The policy aims not only to curb inflation but also supporting growth.
The policy not only aims to curb inflation but also to support growth.
The policy aims at curbing inflation and to support growth.
The policy aims to curb inflation as well as supporting growth.
The policy aims not only to curb inflation but also to support growth.

steps: After 'not only' and 'but also' the same form (to-infinitive) follows, and 'not only' sits right before what it pairs.
The others mismatch forms or misplace 'not only' (it stands before 'aims' but pairs 'to curb' with 'to support').
solution.trap: The second wrong option has the right verbs but 'not only' in the wrong place.
solution.rule: Correlatives (not only … but also, either … or) must be followed by matching forms

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Rushing to catch the train, I let my bag slip off my shoulder.
Weather permitting, the match will begin at nine.
Rushing to catch the train, my bag slipped off my shoulder.
Considering the circumstances, the decision was reasonable.

steps: The opening phrase describes a person, but the subject is 'my bag', so the modifier dangles.
'Weather permitting' is an absolute phrase with its own subject, and 'Considering' works as a preposition here; both are correct.
solution.trap: 'Considering …' and 'Weather permitting' look like dangling phrases but are accepted fixed uses.
solution.rule: Dangling modifier: the subject of the main clause must be the doer of the opening phrase

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Of the two proposals, the second is ______.

steps: With exactly two items the comparative is used, and 'the' is used because the comparison is 'of the two': 'the more practical'.
Completed sentence: *Of the two proposals, the second is the more practical.*
solution.trap: 'the most practical' is used only for three or more.
solution.rule: Comparative, not superlative, when comparing two; 'the' + comparative with 'of the two'

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: She has a flair for languages and speaks French fluently.
The honesty is the best policy.
He is a MBA from a reputed institute.
She is best student in the class.
He was a honest officer throughout his career.

steps: 'a flair for' takes the indefinite article, and names of languages take none.
The others need 'Honesty is' (abstract noun in general), 'an MBA' (M is said 'em'), 'the best student' (superlative), and 'an honest officer' (silent h).
solution.trap: 'a MBA' looks right because M is a consonant letter, but it is said 'em'.
solution.rule: Articles: 'an' before a vowel sound (an MBA, an honest); 'the' before a superlative; none before abstract nouns in general

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The auditor objected ______ the accounts without supporting vouchers.

steps: In 'object to', 'to' is a preposition, so a gerund follows: 'objected to passing'.
Completed sentence: *The auditor objected to passing the accounts without supporting vouchers.*
solution.trap: 'objected to pass' treats 'to' as part of an infinitive.
solution.rule: object to / be averse to / be committed to + -ing

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Few people knew the answer, did they?
Don't forget to lock the door, will you?
There's hardly any milk left, is there?
You'd better leave now, wouldn't you?

steps: 'You'd better' is short for 'You had better', so the tag is 'hadn't you?'.
The others are correct: 'few' and 'hardly' are negative (positive tags), and a negative imperative takes 'will you?'.
solution.trap: The contraction 'd hides 'had'; it is easy to read it as 'would'.
solution.rule: Question tags: 'd better = had better → hadn't you?

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

This is one of the few branches in the district that ______ a locker facility.

steps: 'that' refers to 'branches' (plural): several branches offer lockers, and this is one of them. So the verb is plural: 'offer'.
Completed sentence: *This is one of the few branches in the district that offer a locker facility.*
solution.trap: 'This is one' is singular, which makes 'offers' tempting.
solution.rule: In 'one of the … that / who …', the relative clause verb agrees with the plural noun

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The train arrived lately because of the fog.
The newly appointed officer spoke firmly but politely.
She sings good for a beginner.
He is a hardly worker who never takes leave.
The project was near complete when the funds ran out.

steps: 'newly' modifies the adjective 'appointed', and 'firmly' and 'politely' modify 'spoke'.
The others need 'arrived late' (lately means recently), 'sings well', 'a hard worker', and 'nearly complete'.
solution.trap: 'lately' and 'hardly' are not the adverbs of 'late' and 'hard'.
solution.rule: Adjective vs adverb: late / lately, hard / hardly, near / nearly have different meanings

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The loan was sanctioned in spite of his poor credit history.
She was accused of forging the signature.
The new scheme is on a par with the old one.
He has been working here for the past decade.

steps: All four sentences are correct.
'in spite of', 'accused of + -ing', 'on a par with' (equal to) and 'for the past decade' (a period with the present perfect continuous) are all standard.
solution.trap: A long, formal sentence feels as if it must hide an error, but each preposition here is the fixed, correct one.
solution.rule: Prepositions: in spite of, accused of, on a par with, for + period

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Every morning my father ______ a walk in the park before he leaves for work.

steps: 'Every morning' marks a habit, and 'leaves' keeps the sentence in the present, so the simple present is needed; 'my father' is singular, so 'takes'.
Completed sentence: *Every morning my father takes a walk in the park before he leaves for work.*
solution.trap: 'took' could describe a past habit, but it clashes with 'leaves' in the same sentence; 'is taking' is for an action in progress now.
solution.rule: Simple present for habits and routines

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

______ moon was shining brightly over the lake when we reached the resort.

steps: There is only one moon in our sky, so it takes the definite article: 'The moon'.
Completed sentence: *The moon was shining brightly over the lake when we reached the resort.*
solution.trap: 'A moon' would suggest one of several moons; 'An' is wrong anyway before the consonant sound 'm'.
solution.rule: Articles: 'the' before things that are one of a kind (the sun, the moon, the sky)

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

My little brother is afraid ______ the dark and sleeps with the light on.

steps: The adjective 'afraid' always takes 'of': 'afraid of the dark'.
Completed sentence: *My little brother is afraid of the dark and sleeps with the light on.*
solution.trap: 'afraid from' is a common slip; 'afraid' never takes 'from'.
solution.rule: Adjective + preposition: afraid of, fond of, proud of, aware of

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

There is very ______ milk left in the jug, so please buy a packet on your way home.

steps: 'milk' is uncountable, so it takes 'little' (hardly any); 'few', 'many', 'a few' and 'several' go only with plural countable nouns.
Completed sentence: *There is very little milk left in the jug, so please buy a packet on your way home.*
solution.trap: 'very few' sounds natural, but 'few' cannot go with an uncountable noun like 'milk'.
solution.rule: Quantifiers: little / much with uncountable nouns; few / many with countable plurals

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Would you mind ______ the window? It is very cold in here.

steps: 'mind' is followed by a gerund (-ing form): 'Would you mind closing …?'.
Completed sentence: *Would you mind closing the window? It is very cold in here.*
solution.trap: 'Would you mind to close' is a common error; 'mind' never takes a to-infinitive.
solution.rule: Gerund after mind, enjoy, avoid, finish, keep

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

This bridge over the river ______ by British engineers in 1890.

steps: The bridge did not build anything; it received the action, and 'in 1890' is a finished past time, so the past passive 'was built' is needed.
Completed sentence: *This bridge over the river was built by British engineers in 1890.*
solution.trap: 'built' alone turns the sentence into a fragment with no main verb; 'is built' clashes with 'in 1890'.
solution.rule: Passive voice: be + past participle, in the tense the time marker needs

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

You ______ cooked so much food; only four guests turned up and most of it was wasted.

steps: The food was cooked, but it turned out to be unnecessary. That is exactly what 'needn't have + past participle' expresses.
Completed sentence: *You needn't have cooked so much food; only four guests turned up and most of it was wasted.*
solution.trap: 'needn't', 'didn't need' and 'couldn't' cannot be followed by the past participle 'cooked'; 'mustn't have' does not express an unnecessary past action.
solution.rule: needn't have + past participle: the action was done, but it was not necessary

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Our science teacher told us that the earth ______ around the sun once a year.

steps: A universal truth stays in the simple present even after a past reporting verb like 'told': 'the earth revolves'.
Completed sentence: *Our science teacher told us that the earth revolves around the sun once a year.*
solution.trap: The usual back-shift rule pulls you towards 'revolved', but facts that are always true are not shifted back.
solution.rule: Reported speech: universal truths and scientific facts keep the present tense

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Unless you ______ harder, you will not clear the exam this year.

steps: 'Unless' means 'if not' and introduces a first conditional, so it takes the simple present: 'Unless you work harder'.
Completed sentence: *Unless you work harder, you will not clear the exam this year.*
solution.trap: 'Unless you don't work' is a double negative; 'unless' already contains the 'not'.
solution.rule: Unless = if not; it takes the simple present here and never takes another 'not'

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

I wish I ______ the bus this morning; I would not have been late for the interview.

steps: The regret is about a past event ('this morning', 'would not have been late'), so 'wish' takes the past perfect: 'hadn't missed'.
Completed sentence: *I wish I hadn't missed the bus this morning; I would not have been late for the interview.*
solution.trap: 'didn't miss' after 'wish' refers to the present, not to something that has already happened.
solution.rule: wish + past perfect for regret about the past; wish + past simple for the present

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

It is high time the municipality ______ the potholes on this road.

steps: 'It is high time' is followed by the past simple (with present meaning) to say that something should already have been done: 'repaired'.
Completed sentence: *It is high time the municipality repaired the potholes on this road.*
solution.trap: The sentence is about the present, which makes 'repairs' look right, but this structure needs the past form.
solution.rule: It is (high / about) time + subject + past simple

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

When we lived in Shimla, we ______ walk to school through the pine forest.

steps: A past habit that no longer continues takes 'used to + base verb': 'we used to walk'.
Completed sentence: *When we lived in Shimla, we used to walk to school through the pine forest.*
solution.trap: 'were used to' means 'were accustomed to' and would need 'walking'; 'use to' without -d is wrong in a positive sentence.
solution.rule: used to + base verb = past habit; be used to + -ing = be accustomed to

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Neither of the brothers turned up for the wedding, ______?

steps: 'Neither' makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive; 'Neither of the brothers' is picked up by 'they', and 'turned up' takes 'did': 'did they?'.
Completed sentence: *Neither of the brothers turned up for the wedding, did they?*
solution.trap: There is no 'not' in the sentence, so a negative tag like 'didn't they' looks right.
solution.rule: Question tags: neither, nobody, never, hardly → positive tag; neither of / nobody → they

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Our car was making a strange noise, so we ______ at the service centre yesterday.

steps: Someone else checked the car for us, so the causative 'have + object + past participle' is used, in the past because of 'yesterday': 'had it checked'.
Completed sentence: *Our car was making a strange noise, so we had it checked at the service centre yesterday.*
solution.trap: 'have it checked' has the right pattern but the wrong tense for 'yesterday'.
solution.rule: Causative: have / get + object + past participle (have it checked, get it repaired)

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The application form must ______ before 5 p.m. on Friday.

steps: The form does not submit anything; it is submitted. After a modal the passive is 'be + past participle': 'must be submitted'.
Completed sentence: *The application form must be submitted before 5 p.m. on Friday.*
solution.trap: 'must submit' would make the form the doer of the action.
solution.rule: Passive with modals: modal + be + past participle

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Although it was my turn, my friend insisted ______ the bill at the restaurant.

steps: 'insist' takes the preposition 'on', and a preposition is followed by a gerund: 'insisted on paying'.
Completed sentence: *Although it was my turn, my friend insisted on paying the bill at the restaurant.*
solution.trap: 'insisted to pay' is a common error carried over from 'wanted to pay'.
solution.rule: insist on / persist in / succeed in + -ing

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The news about the floods in Assam ______ shocked everyone in our village.

steps: 'news' looks plural but is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb: 'The news … has shocked'.
Completed sentence: *The news about the floods in Assam has shocked everyone in our village.*
solution.trap: The final -s and the plural 'floods' both pull you towards 'have'.
solution.rule: Nouns ending in -s that are singular: news, mathematics, physics, measles

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

This is the farmer ______ land was taken over for the new highway.

steps: The land belongs to the farmer, so the possessive relative pronoun 'whose' is needed: 'the farmer whose land'.
Completed sentence: *This is the farmer whose land was taken over for the new highway.*
solution.trap: 'who' and 'whom' refer to the farmer himself, not to something he owns.
solution.rule: Relative pronouns: whose shows possession (the man whose car …)

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

On the doctor's advice, my uncle stopped ______ ten years ago and has not touched a cigarette since.

steps: He gave up the habit, so 'stop' takes a gerund: 'stopped smoking'.
Completed sentence: *On the doctor's advice, my uncle stopped smoking ten years ago and has not touched a cigarette since.*
solution.trap: 'stopped to smoke' means he paused in order to have a smoke, which contradicts 'has not touched a cigarette since'.
solution.rule: stop + -ing = give up an activity; stop + to-infinitive = pause in order to do something

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

This new model is far superior ______ the old one in fuel efficiency.

steps: Latin comparatives such as superior, inferior, senior, junior and prior take 'to', not 'than'.
Completed sentence: *This new model is far superior to the old one in fuel efficiency.*
solution.trap: 'superior' sounds like a comparative, so 'than' feels natural.
solution.rule: superior / inferior / senior / junior / prior + to

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The more you practise the piano, ______ you will become.

steps: The pattern 'the + comparative …, the + comparative …' shows two things changing together, so the second half also needs 'the more confident'.
Completed sentence: *The more you practise the piano, the more confident you will become.*
solution.trap: Dropping 'the' in the second half ('more confident') is the usual slip.
solution.rule: The + comparative …, the + comparative … (the more …, the more …)

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

______ of the two candidates was given ten minutes to present a plan.

steps: With two people and a singular verb ('was given'), 'Each of' is right; it takes the two one at a time.
Completed sentence: *Each of the two candidates was given ten minutes to present a plan.*
solution.trap: 'Every' cannot be followed by 'of' and is not used for two; 'All' and 'Both' would need 'were'.
solution.rule: Quantifiers: each (two or more, singular verb); every (three or more, never 'every of')

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The officer asked me why ______ late for the interview.

steps: A reported question uses statement word order (subject before verb), and the past reporting verb 'asked' shifts the tense back: 'why I was late'.
Completed sentence: *The officer asked me why I was late for the interview.*
solution.trap: 'was I' copies the word order of the direct question 'Why are you late?'.
solution.rule: Reported questions: no inversion, no question mark; tense shifts back after a past reporting verb

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The lights went out while we ______ dinner.

steps: A longer action in progress ('while we …') interrupted by a short past action ('went out') takes the past continuous: 'were having'.
Completed sentence: *The lights went out while we were having dinner.*
solution.trap: 'are having' is in the present and clashes with 'went'.
solution.rule: Past continuous for an action in progress when another past action happened

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Please remember ______ the gas cylinder before you leave for the weekend.

steps: This is a duty still to be done, so 'remember' takes the to-infinitive: 'remember to turn off'.
Completed sentence: *Please remember to turn off the gas cylinder before you leave for the weekend.*
solution.trap: 'remember turning off' would refer to a memory of something already done, which does not fit 'before you leave'.
solution.rule: remember / forget + to-infinitive = a future duty; + -ing = a memory of a past action

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

I would rather you ______ the matter to anyone outside the office until the deal is signed.

steps: When 'would rather' is followed by a different subject ('you'), the verb is in the past simple even though the meaning is present or future: 'I would rather you didn't mention'.
Completed sentence: *I would rather you didn't mention the matter to anyone outside the office until the deal is signed.*
solution.trap: The meaning is about now and the future, so 'don't mention' feels right, but this structure needs the past form.
solution.rule: would rather + another subject + past simple (I'd rather you stayed)

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The bank had already waived the fee, so I ______ anything at the counter; I simply collected my cheque book and left.

steps: No payment was made because none was required. 'didn't need to + verb' says only that something was not necessary.
Completed sentence: *The bank had already waived the fee, so I didn't need to pay anything at the counter; I simply collected my cheque book and left.*
solution.trap: 'needn't have paid' means I did pay, unnecessarily, which contradicts 'simply collected my cheque book and left'.
solution.rule: didn't need to = it was not necessary (usually not done); needn't have + past participle = done, though unnecessary

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

______ any difficulty while logging in, please call our helpline.

steps: 'Should you face' is an inverted first conditional (= If you face), which fits a polite instruction about the future.
Completed sentence: *Should you face any difficulty while logging in, please call our helpline.*
solution.trap: 'Had you faced' is a third conditional about the past and cannot be followed by the instruction 'please call'.
solution.rule: Inverted conditional: Should + subject + base verb (= If + subject + present)

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Not until the results were declared ______ how close the contest had been.

steps: When 'Not until …' begins a sentence, the main clause is inverted with an auxiliary: 'did we realise'.
Completed sentence: *Not until the results were declared did we realise how close the contest had been.*
solution.trap: 'we realised' is the normal word order, which is correct only when 'not until' comes later: 'We did not realise … until …'.
solution.rule: Inversion after a fronted negative: Not until / Never / Seldom / Only then + auxiliary + subject

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Last year he saved every rupee so that he ______ buy his mother a house before she retired.

steps: The main verb 'saved' is past, so the purpose clause takes the past form of the modal: 'so that he might (or could) buy'.
Completed sentence: *Last year he saved every rupee so that he might buy his mother a house before she retired.*
solution.trap: 'so that he may' is the present pattern and breaks the sequence of tenses after 'saved'.
solution.rule: Sequence of tenses: past main verb → might / could in the 'so that' clause

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

We regret ______ you that your application has not been shortlisted for the next round.

steps: The bad news is being given now, so 'regret' takes the to-infinitive: 'regret to inform you'.
Completed sentence: *We regret to inform you that your application has not been shortlisted for the next round.*
solution.trap: 'regret informing you' would mean being sorry that you informed someone earlier, not giving news now.
solution.rule: regret + to-infinitive = sorry to say now; regret + -ing = sorry about a past action

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The committee ______ divided in their opinions, so no decision could be taken.

steps: The members are acting as separate individuals with different opinions ('their opinions'), so the collective noun takes a plural verb: 'were'.
Completed sentence: *The committee were divided in their opinions, so no decision could be taken.*
solution.trap: 'The committee was' is right when it acts as one body, but 'divided in their opinions' makes it plural.
solution.rule: Collective nouns: singular verb when acting as one unit, plural when the members act separately

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The officer, ______ I believed to be honest, turned out to be corrupt.

steps: The pronoun is the object of 'believed' (I believed him to be honest), so the object form 'whom' is needed.
Completed sentence: *The officer, whom I believed to be honest, turned out to be corrupt.*
solution.trap: 'who' would be right in 'who I believed was honest', where it is the subject of 'was'; with 'to be' it is the object. 'that' cannot open a clause set off by commas.
solution.rule: Relative pronouns: whom is the object (I believed him → whom I believed to be)

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

We still have ______ time before the train leaves, so let us have a cup of tea.

steps: There is some time, enough for tea, so the positive 'a little' is needed with the uncountable noun 'time'.
Completed sentence: *We still have a little time before the train leaves, so let us have a cup of tea.*
solution.trap: 'little time' means hardly any time, which contradicts stopping for tea.
solution.rule: a little = some (positive); little = hardly any (negative); both with uncountable nouns

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The new flyover ______ when the contractor ran out of funds, so it was left half-finished.

steps: The flyover was in the middle of receiving the action when the funds ran out, so the past continuous passive is needed: 'was being built'.
Completed sentence: *The new flyover was being built when the contractor ran out of funds, so it was left half-finished.*
solution.trap: 'was building' is active and would make the flyover the builder.
solution.rule: Past continuous passive: was / were + being + past participle

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

If only I ______ to my father's advice last year, I would not be in this mess now.

steps: The regret is about a past action ('last year'), so 'If only' takes the past perfect; the present result ('now') makes it a mixed conditional.
Completed sentence: *If only I had listened to my father's advice last year, I would not be in this mess now.*
solution.trap: 'listened' after 'If only' refers to the present, which clashes with 'last year'.
solution.rule: If only + past perfect for a past regret (mixed with a present result: would + verb … now)

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

He moved to Bengaluru with a view to ______ a software start-up.

steps: In 'with a view to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by a gerund: 'with a view to starting'.
Completed sentence: *He moved to Bengaluru with a view to starting a software start-up.*
solution.trap: 'to start' looks like a normal infinitive of purpose, but 'with a view to' must be followed by -ing.
solution.rule: with a view to / look forward to / be used to + -ing

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

By the time the ambulance arrives, the injured man ______ a lot of blood.

steps: 'By the time' + a future event needs an action completed before that point: the future perfect 'will have lost'.
Completed sentence: *By the time the ambulance arrives, the injured man will have lost a lot of blood.*
solution.trap: 'will lose' does not show that the loss is complete before the ambulance arrives.
solution.rule: Future perfect (will have + past participle) with 'by the time' / 'by then' in the future

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

After a lot of persuasion, I finally got my brother ______ me with the shifting.

steps: 'get' + person takes a to-infinitive when you persuade someone to act: 'got my brother to help me'.
Completed sentence: *After a lot of persuasion, I finally got my brother to help me with the shifting.*
solution.trap: 'got my brother help me' borrows the bare infinitive that only 'have' and 'make' take.
solution.rule: Causative: get + person + to-infinitive; have / make + person + bare infinitive

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Only after the auditors had gone through every voucher ______.

steps: A sentence that opens with 'Only after …' inverts the main clause, and the accounts receive the action (passive): 'were the accounts approved'.
Completed sentence: *Only after the auditors had gone through every voucher were the accounts approved.*
solution.trap: 'the accounts were approved' is a correct passive but misses the inversion; 'did the accounts approve' inverts but makes the accounts the approvers.
solution.rule: Inversion after 'Only after / Only when / Only then'; in the passive the auxiliary 'were' moves before the subject

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

But for the timely help of the fishermen that night, the passengers of the capsized boat ______.

steps: 'But for' means 'if it had not been for', and 'that night' places it in the past, so the result is 'would have + past participle'.
Completed sentence: *But for the timely help of the fishermen that night, the passengers of the capsized boat would have drowned.*
solution.trap: 'would drown' is the present-unreal form and does not fit an event that happened 'that night'.
solution.rule: But for + noun (= if it had not been for) → would have + past participle for a past event

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

More than one bank ______ revised its lending rates this month.

steps: 'More than one' followed by a singular noun ('bank') takes a singular verb; 'its' confirms the singular: 'has revised'.
Completed sentence: *More than one bank has revised its lending rates this month.*
solution.trap: 'More than one' means at least two banks, so the plural 'have' feels logical.
solution.rule: More than one + singular noun → singular verb

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

______ the warning in time, the accident would not have happened.

steps: 'would not have happened' needs an inverted third conditional (= If the driver had heeded); heeding the warning is what would have prevented the accident.
Completed sentence: *Had the driver heeded the warning in time, the accident would not have happened.*
solution.trap: 'Had the driver not heeded' is grammatical but reverses the logic: ignoring the warning would not have prevented the accident.
solution.rule: Inverted third conditional: Had + subject + past participle, would have + past participle

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The longer the meeting dragged on, ______.
options: the less attentive the members became
the less the members became attentive
the lesser attentive the members became

steps: The first half is 'the + comparative', so the second half must match it: 'the less attentive the members became', with the comparative phrase first and the subject after it.
Completed sentence: *The longer the meeting dragged on, the less attentive the members became.*
solution.trap: 'the members became less attentive' is a normal sentence but breaks the 'the …, the …' pattern.
solution.rule: The + comparative + subject + verb, the + comparative + subject + verb

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

You ought ______ the doctor before you started taking those tablets.

steps: 'started' shows that the chance has already passed, so a past duty that was not done takes 'ought to have + past participle'.
Completed sentence: *You ought to have consulted the doctor before you started taking those tablets.*
solution.trap: 'ought to consult' is advice for now or the future and clashes with 'started'; 'ought have' drops the 'to'.
solution.rule: ought to have + past participle = a past duty that was not carried out

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: She bought a umbrella from the market.
He is an useful member of the team.
I saw a owl sitting on the tree last night.
It was an unusual sight for the villagers.
She has a eye for detail.

steps: 'unusual' begins with a vowel sound ('un'), so 'an unusual sight' is correct.
The others need 'an umbrella', 'a useful' ('yoo' is a consonant sound), 'an owl' and 'an eye'.
solution.trap: 'useful' starts with the letter u, but the sound is 'yoo', so it takes 'a'.
solution.rule: Articles: 'an' before a vowel sound, 'a' before a consonant sound

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: We were watching a film when the guests arrived.
They was playing cricket when it started to rain.
He has gone to Chennai last week.
Yesterday I meet my old teacher at the bus stand.

steps: The past continuous ('were watching') shows the longer action that the guests' arrival interrupted.
The others need 'doesn't like', 'were playing', 'went to Chennai last week' (no present perfect with a finished time) and 'met'.
solution.trap: 'has gone … last week' looks fine, but a finished past time needs the simple past.
solution.rule: Tenses: past continuous + simple past for an interrupted action

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: She prefers to read than to watch television.
I prefer walking to taking an auto for short distances.
They would prefer staying at home than going out.
She would rather to stay at home than go out.
This hotel is preferable than that one.

steps: 'prefer + -ing … to + -ing' is the correct pattern: 'prefer walking to taking'.
The others need 'prefers to read rather than watch', 'would prefer to stay at home rather than go out', 'would rather stay' (no 'to') and 'preferable to'.
solution.trap: 'than' feels natural after any preference, but 'prefer' and 'preferable' take 'to'.
solution.rule: prefer X to Y; prefer to do X rather than do Y; would rather do X than do Y; preferable to

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: He said that he will come the next day.
She asked me if I can help her with the project.
The teacher told us that light travels faster than sound.
He told that he was too tired to go out.
She told to me that she was busy.

steps: A scientific fact stays in the present after 'told', and 'told' correctly has its object 'us'.
The others need 'would come' and 'could help' (back-shift after a past reporting verb), 'told me that' or 'said that', and 'told me' (no 'to').
solution.trap: 'said' and 'told' are not interchangeable: 'told' needs a person as object, 'said' does not take one directly.
solution.rule: Reported speech: will → would, can → could; tell + person, say (to) + person

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The letter has been wrote by my sister.
A new school is build in our village.
The work will finished by tomorrow.
The match was being watched by thousands of fans.

steps: The past continuous passive 'was being + past participle' is formed correctly.
The others need 'has been written', 'is being built' (or 'has been built'), 'will be finished' and 'was delivered'.
solution.trap: Every wrong sentence uses the wrong verb form after the auxiliary; check for be + past participle.
solution.rule: Passive voice: a form of 'be' + past participle

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: You ought to apologise to your sister.
You must to wear a helmet while riding.
She needs not worry about the fees.

steps: 'ought' is the one modal that takes 'to': 'ought to apologise'.
The others need 'must wear', 'can sing', 'need not worry' (or 'does not need to worry') and 'should have gone'.
solution.trap: 'ought to' makes 'must to' look acceptable, but other modals take the bare infinitive.
solution.rule: Modals take the base verb; 'ought' is followed by 'to'

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The boy which won the race is my neighbour.
This is the house where I was born in.
The pen who I lost was a gift from my aunt.
The doctor whom I consulted was very kind.
My mother, that is a nurse, works night shifts.

steps: 'whom' is the object of 'consulted' and refers to a person, so it is correct.
The others need 'who won' (a person), 'where I was born' (or 'which I was born in'), 'which/that I lost' (a thing) and 'who is a nurse' ('that' cannot begin a clause set off by commas).
solution.trap: 'where … in' says the place twice.
solution.rule: Relative pronouns: who / whom for people, which for things, that not after a comma

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: I am used to wake up early.
He didn't use to like vegetables as a child.
She used to living in a hostel.
They are use to the noise of the traffic.
We use to play cricket every Sunday when we were young.

steps: After 'didn't' the base form 'use to' is correct, and it describes a past habit.
The others need 'used to waking up', 'used to live', 'are used to the noise' and 'used to play'.
solution.trap: 'used to' and 'be used to' look alike; only 'be used to' is followed by -ing or a noun.
solution.rule: used to + base verb (past habit); be / get used to + -ing or noun (accustomed)

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Neither of the three brothers came to the wedding.
Every students must carry an identity card.
He has a few money left in his account.
Either of the two roads leads to the market.

steps: 'Either' is used for two and takes a singular verb: 'Either of the two roads leads'.
The others need 'None of the three' ('neither' is only for two), 'Every student', 'a little money' and 'Many people'.
solution.trap: 'Neither of the three' sounds fine, but 'either' and 'neither' refer to exactly two.
solution.rule: Quantifiers: either / neither for two; none for three or more; every + singular noun

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: She is coming tomorrow, isn't it?
They went to Ooty last month, didn't it?
You have finished your homework, haven't you?
He never tells lies, doesn't he?
Rahul works in a bank, isn't he?

steps: The tag repeats the helping verb 'have' with the opposite polarity and the same subject: 'haven't you?'.
The others need 'isn't she?', 'didn't they?', 'does he?' (never is negative) and 'doesn't he?' (works → does).
solution.trap: 'isn't it?' is used in speech as an all-purpose tag, but the tag must match the subject and the verb.
solution.rule: Question tags repeat the auxiliary and the subject pronoun, with the opposite polarity

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: I got my hair cut at the new salon yesterday.
I had my bicycle repair at the shop near the station.
She had the room clean by the maid.
We have our house painting every year.
He had his photograph take for the passport.

steps: Someone else cut the hair, so 'get + object + past participle' is correct; 'cut' is also the past participle.
The others need 'repaired', 'cleaned', 'painted' and 'taken': the causative uses the past participle.
solution.trap: 'cut' looks like the base form, which makes the right sentence seem wrong.
solution.rule: Causative: have / get + object + past participle

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: I remember to meet him at a wedding years ago.
He suggested to go for a walk after dinner.
We tried pushing the car, but it still would not start.
Don't forget posting the letter on your way to the office.
She regrets to shout at her son yesterday.

steps: 'try + -ing' means trying something as an experiment to see if it works, which fits a car that would not start.
The others need 'remember meeting' (a memory), 'suggested going', 'forget to post' (a duty still to be done) and 'regrets shouting' (a past action).
solution.trap: 'remember', 'forget' and 'regret' take either form, but the form changes the meaning; time words like 'years ago' and 'yesterday' decide it.
solution.rule: remember / forget / regret + -ing = past action; + to-infinitive = future duty or present announcement

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: If I had known about the strike, I would not come to the office yesterday.
Were I in your place, I would accept the offer.
If he would have asked me, I would have helped him.
Had she left early, she will catch the train.
Should you needed any help, call me.

steps: 'Were I in your place' is an inverted second conditional (= If I were in your place), correctly followed by 'would accept'.
The others need 'would not have come', 'If he had asked', 'she would have caught' and 'Should you need'.
solution.trap: 'If he would have asked' puts 'would' in the if-clause, a common error.
solution.rule: Inverted conditionals: Were + subject; Had + subject + past participle; Should + subject + base verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: I wish I can speak French fluently.
I would rather you stayed with us tonight.
It is high time we leave for the station.
If only he has listened to me!
She wishes she has more free time.

steps: 'would rather' with another subject takes the past simple for a present or future wish: 'you stayed'.
The others need 'I wish I could speak', 'high time we left', 'If only he had listened' and 'wishes she had'.
solution.trap: All five sentences are about the present or future, which makes present forms tempting; these structures need past forms.
solution.rule: wish / if only / it's high time / would rather (+ another subject) → past form

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Never I have seen such a beautiful sunset.
Rarely we get such an opportunity.
Not only he sings well but he also dances.
Hardly the bell had rung when the students rushed out.
Seldom have I seen such a large crowd at a book fair.

steps: 'Seldom' at the start of the sentence is followed by the auxiliary before the subject: 'Seldom have I seen'.
The others need 'Never have I seen', 'Rarely do we get', 'Not only does he sing well' and 'Hardly had the bell rung'.
solution.trap: Each wrong sentence uses the normal word order after a negative adverb.
solution.rule: Inversion after a fronted negative adverb: Seldom / Never / Rarely / Hardly / Not only + auxiliary + subject

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Many a student has failed this paper.
The furniture in these rooms are new.
The police has arrested the culprit.
The cattle is grazing in the field.

steps: 'Many a' is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb: 'Many a student has'.
The others need 'furniture … is' (uncountable), 'Physics is', 'The police have' and 'The cattle are' (always plural).
solution.trap: 'Many a' means many people, so a plural verb feels logical.
solution.rule: Agreement: many a + singular; furniture, physics → singular; police, cattle → plural

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Everyone except she was invited to the party.
Ravi and myself will handle the accounts.
Us students were asked to stay back after class.
The manager asked Priya and I to stay late.
She trusted no one but him.

steps: 'but' here means 'except' and is a preposition, so the object form 'him' is correct.
The others need 'except her' (object after a preposition), 'Ravi and I' (subject), 'We students' (subject) and 'Priya and me' (object of 'asked').
solution.trap: 'myself' sounds polite but is used only when the subject does the action to itself or for emphasis.
solution.rule: Pronoun case: subject form for subjects; object form after verbs and prepositions (except, but, between)

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Of the two brothers, Ramesh is the tallest.
Iron is more useful than any other metal.
He is the most cleverest boy in the class.
The population of Mumbai is larger than Pune.
My cousin is elder than me by three years.

steps: Iron is itself a metal, so it is compared with 'any other metal'.
The others need 'the taller' (two people), 'the cleverest' (no double superlative), 'than that of Pune' (population with population) and 'older than' ('elder' is not used with 'than').
solution.trap: Each wrong sentence looks natural in speech; check the number of things compared and what is being compared.
solution.rule: Comparison: 'any other' within the same group; comparative for two; compare like with like

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The Mount Everest is the highest peak in the world.
He goes to the bed at ten every night.
She is the best singer in our college.
They travelled by the train to Jaipur.

steps: A superlative ('best') takes 'the'.
The others need 'Mount Everest' (single peaks take no article), 'goes to bed' (its main purpose), 'The sun' (unique object) and 'by train' (means of transport).
solution.trap: 'the Himalayas' takes 'the', but a single peak like Mount Everest does not.
solution.rule: Articles: 'the' with superlatives and unique objects; none with single peaks, 'go to bed', 'by train'

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: He told me that he has finished the work.
I will call you when I will reach home.
I am waiting here for two hours.
He said he would join us after he had finished his lunch.
We have shifted to this flat two years ago.

steps: After the past 'said', 'will' becomes 'would', and the earlier action takes the past perfect 'had finished'.
The others need 'had finished' (back-shift after 'told'), 'when I reach' (no 'will' in a time clause), 'have been waiting' (duration up to now) and 'shifted … two years ago' (finished time).
solution.trap: 'when I will reach' puts a future form in a time clause, where English uses the present.
solution.rule: Sequence of tenses: past reporting verb → past forms; present tense in time clauses about the future

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: We needn't have booked the tickets in advance; the hall was half empty when we got there.
The office was closed for the festival, so he needn't have gone to work and he spent the day at home.
You needn't to bring your laptop tomorrow.
She didn't need to taken a loan for the course.
They need not had worried about the results.

steps: The tickets were booked, and it turned out to be unnecessary, so 'needn't have booked' is right.
The first wrong sentence needs 'didn't need to go': he stayed at home, but 'needn't have gone' says he went. The others need 'needn't bring', 'didn't need to take' and 'need not have worried'.
solution.trap: The office sentence is grammatical in form but says the opposite of what happened.
solution.rule: needn't have + past participle = done but unnecessary; didn't need to + verb = not necessary (usually not done)

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Not until he apologised she forgave him.
Under no circumstances you should share your PIN.
Had I not seen it myself, I would not have believed it.
Only then I understood the problem.
So loud the music was that we could not talk.

steps: 'Had I not seen' is an inverted third conditional (= If I had not seen), correctly followed by 'would not have believed'.
The others need 'did she forgive him', 'should you share', 'did I understand' and 'So loud was the music'.
solution.trap: Each wrong sentence opens like an inversion but keeps the normal word order after it.
solution.rule: Inversion after Not until / Under no circumstances / Only then / So + adjective, and in conditionals without 'if'

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The jewellery she wore at the wedding were her grandmother's.
Neither the principal nor the teachers was present.
One of the reasons for the delays were the strike.
The scenery of Kashmir are breathtaking.
None of the money collected was spent on the project.

steps: 'None of' + an uncountable noun ('money') takes a singular verb.
The others need 'was' (jewellery is uncountable), 'were' (the nearer subject 'teachers' is plural), 'was' (the subject is 'One') and 'is' (scenery is uncountable).
solution.trap: 'the delays' and 'the strike' surround the verb, but its subject is 'One'.
solution.rule: Agreement: uncountable nouns → singular; neither … nor → nearer subject; one of … → singular

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: He is the only one of the officers who have refused the bribe.
The man whom I thought was a thief turned out to be a detective.
The book which cover is torn belongs to Rahul.
The colleague with whom I share a cabin has been transferred to Nagpur.
The students, that had failed, were asked to reappear.

steps: After a preposition the object form 'whom' is used: 'with whom I share a cabin'.
The others need 'who has refused' ('the only one' is singular), 'who I thought was' (subject of 'was'), 'whose cover' and 'who had failed' ('that' cannot follow a comma).
solution.trap: In 'the only one of the officers who …', the clause refers to the one officer, unlike 'one of the officers who'.
solution.rule: Relative clauses: whom after a preposition; 'the only one of … who' → singular verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: She said that she is going to Mumbai the next day.
The teacher asked the students that why they were late.
He said me that he would call later.
Ravi asked his friend where was the bank.
He asked me whether I had seen the film the previous day.

steps: A yes/no question is reported with 'whether', and the past 'saw … yesterday' becomes 'had seen … the previous day'.
The others need 'was going … the next day', 'asked the students why' (no 'that'), 'told me' or 'said to me', and 'where the bank was'.
solution.trap: 'is going' is tempting if the trip is still ahead, but 'the next day' shows that the time words have been shifted, so the tense must shift too.
solution.rule: Reported speech: back-shift tense and time words together; reported questions take statement word order

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: My sister and I go to the same school.
The children is playing in the garden.
He has two dogs and a cat.

steps: 'children' is plural, so the verb must be 'are playing'.
The others are correct: 'My sister and I' takes 'go', 'He has', 'The shop opens'.
solution.trap: 'children' has no final -s, so it can be mistaken for a singular noun.
solution.rule: Subject–verb agreement: plural subject → plural verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: She is married to a doctor.
We are proud of our team.
He was angry on his son for lying.
The bus was full of tourists.

steps: One is angry 'with' a person (and 'at' or 'about' a thing): 'angry with his son'.
The others use the correct fixed prepositions: married to, proud of, full of.
solution.trap: 'married with' and 'angry on' are both common slips; only the second appears here.
solution.rule: Adjective + preposition: angry with (a person), married to, proud of, full of

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: I have been learning the guitar for six months.
She had left before I arrived.
They will be travelling all night.
