steps: 'in 2019' is a finished past time, so the simple past is needed: 'We visited Jaipur in 2019'.
The others are correct: present perfect continuous with 'for', past perfect for the earlier past action, and future continuous.
solution.trap: The present perfect is right for experiences, but not with a stated finished time.
solution.rule: No present perfect with a finished past time (yesterday, in 2019, last week)

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: If you mix blue and yellow, you get green.
If I won the lottery, I would buy a farm.
If she had asked, I would have told her.
If I was knowing the answer, I would tell you.

steps: 'know' is a state verb and is not used in the continuous; a second conditional needs 'If I knew the answer'.
The others are correct zero, second and third conditionals.
solution.trap: 'would tell' is right, so the error hides in the if-clause.
solution.rule: Second conditional: If + past simple, would + verb; state verbs (know, believe) are not used in -ing forms

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The cake was ate by the children.
English is spoken all over the world.
The roads are being repaired this week.

steps: The passive needs the past participle: 'The cake was eaten'.
The others use correct past participles: caught, spoken, being repaired.
solution.trap: 'ate' is the past simple; only the third form (eaten) goes after 'was'.
solution.rule: Passive voice: be + past participle (eat – ate – eaten)

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: You need not fill the form again; the earlier one is still valid.
He can't have taken the money; he was in Delhi that day.
You should to consult a lawyer before signing.
How dare you open my letters?

steps: 'should' is a modal and takes the bare infinitive: 'You should consult'.
The others are correct: 'need not' and 'dare' work as modals with a bare infinitive, and 'can't have taken' is a past deduction.
solution.trap: 'need not fill' and 'How dare you open' look as if they are missing 'to', but as modals they take none.
solution.rule: Modals (should, must, can, need, dare) + bare infinitive; only 'ought' takes 'to'

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: She is interested in learning Sanskrit.
He decided to join the army.
They finished painting the house in two days.
I am thinking to buy a new scooter.

steps: 'think' in this sense takes 'of' + gerund: 'I am thinking of buying'.
The others are correct: 'interested in' + -ing, 'decide to', 'finish' + -ing.
solution.trap: 'thinking to' is a common error because 'planning to' is correct.
solution.rule: think of / interested in / finish + -ing; decide / plan + to-infinitive

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Your brother works in a bank, isn't it?
There are fifty seats in this hall, aren't there?
You are coming with us, aren't you?
Nothing can stop him now, can it?

steps: 'works' has no helping verb, so the tag uses 'does', with 'he' for 'your brother': 'doesn't he?'.
The others are correct: 'There are' → 'aren't there?', 'You are' → 'aren't you?', and 'Nothing' (negative, a thing) → 'can it?'.
solution.trap: 'isn't it?' is common in spoken Indian English but is not a correct tag here.
solution.rule: Question tags: do / does / did when the statement has no helping verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: She is the eldest of the three sisters.
We went to the Ooty for a holiday.

steps: Names of towns and cities take no article: 'We went to Ooty'.
The others are correct: 'the' with a superlative, 'A dog' (any dog), 'an orange' (vowel sound).
solution.trap: 'the Nilgiris' takes 'the', but a single town does not.
solution.rule: Articles: no article before names of towns, cities and most countries

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The students who passed were given certificates.
Do you know the lady whom is standing at the gate?
This is the girl whose father is a pilot.
The book that I borrowed from the library is very interesting.

steps: The pronoun is the subject of 'is standing', so it must be 'who', not 'whom'.
The others are correct: 'who' as a subject, 'whose' for possession and 'that' as an object in a defining clause.
solution.trap: 'whom' sounds formal and correct, but it is only for objects.
solution.rule: Relative pronouns: who = subject, whom = object, whose = possession

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Each student was given a laptop.
She has fewer friends than her brother.
I have a little money; let us buy some snacks.
Every one of the boys were present.

steps: 'Every one of' takes a singular verb: 'Every one of the boys was present'.
The others are correct: 'Each student was', 'fewer friends' (countable), 'a little money' (some, uncountable).
solution.trap: 'boys' stands right before the verb, but the subject is 'Every one'.
solution.rule: Quantifiers: each / every (one) of + plural noun → singular verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: He is used to drive on the left.
My grandfather used to tell us stories every night.
I am not used to eating dinner so late.
She soon got used to the cold.

steps: 'be used to' means 'be accustomed to', and its 'to' is a preposition, so it takes -ing: 'He is used to driving'.
The others are correct: 'used to tell' (past habit), 'used to eating' and 'got used to the cold'.
solution.trap: 'used to + verb' is right for a past habit, which makes 'is used to drive' look acceptable.
solution.rule: be / get used to + -ing or noun; used to + base verb (past habit)

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: We had the roof repaired before the monsoon.
She got her passport renewed last month.
He got his car wash at the petrol pump.
I will have the gardener cut the grass.

steps: In a causative with the thing as object, the verb is the past participle: 'got his car washed'.
The others are correct: have / get + thing + past participle, and have + person + bare infinitive ('have the gardener cut').
solution.trap: 'have the gardener cut' uses the base verb correctly because the object is a person who does the job.
solution.rule: Causative: have / get + thing + past participle; have + person + base verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: He and I have known each other for years.
Please send the documents to myself by Friday.
The decision is yours to make.

steps: A reflexive pronoun is used only when the subject acts on itself or for emphasis; here the object form is needed: 'send the documents to me'.
The others are correct: 'He and I' as subject, the possessive 'yours', and 'themselves' for emphasis.
solution.trap: 'myself' sounds more polite, which is why it is misused for 'me'.
solution.rule: Pronouns: reflexive (myself) only when it refers back to the subject or adds emphasis

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: She said that she was tired after the journey.
He asked me what time it was.
The teacher ordered the boy to stand up.
Ravi said that he has bought a new phone the previous week.

steps: After the past 'said', and with the shifted time phrase 'the previous week', the tense must shift back: 'he had bought'.
The others are correct: back-shifted 'was', statement word order in 'what time it was', and an order reported with 'to stand up'.
solution.trap: 'the previous week' is already back-shifted, which makes the unshifted 'has bought' easy to miss.
solution.rule: Reported speech: past reporting verb → past perfect for an earlier action

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Had they invited us, we would go to the wedding last week.
Had we left earlier, we would have caught the train.
If he had saved money then, he would be rich now.
Should it rain, the match will be postponed.

steps: 'Had they invited us' and 'last week' are both past, so the result must be 'we would have gone'.
The others are correct: an inverted third conditional, a mixed conditional ('then' → 'now'), and an inverted first conditional.
solution.trap: The mixed conditional is correct because of 'now'; the wedding sentence has no 'now' and refers to last week.
solution.rule: Third conditional: Had + subject + past participle → would have + past participle

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: I wish I had more time to read.
It is high time you took your studies seriously.
She would rather that you don't call her after ten.
If only I had known about it earlier!

steps: 'would rather' with another subject takes the past simple: 'She would rather you didn't call her after ten'.
The others are correct: 'wish' + past for the present, 'high time' + past, 'If only' + past perfect for the past.
solution.trap: The meaning is present or future, so 'don't call' feels natural.
solution.rule: would rather + another subject + past simple

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: No sooner had she sat down than the phone rang.
Never before I had seen such dedication.
Only when the rain stopped did we leave.
Little did he know what lay ahead.

steps: A fronted negative adverb ('Never before') needs the auxiliary before the subject: 'Never before had I seen such dedication'.
The others are correct inversions after 'No sooner', 'Only when …' and 'Little'.
solution.trap: The tense is right, so only the word order is wrong.
solution.rule: Inversion after a negative adverb at the start: auxiliary + subject + verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: I remember meeting her at the conference last year.
He stopped to buy some flowers on the way home.
She regrets telling him the secret.
We will never forget to visit Kashmir last summer.

steps: A memory of a past event ('last summer') takes 'forget + -ing': 'We will never forget visiting Kashmir'.
The others are correct: 'remember meeting' (a memory), 'stopped to buy' (paused in order to buy) and 'regrets telling' (a past action).
solution.trap: 'stopped to buy' looks like the classic error, but here it correctly means stopping in order to buy.
solution.rule: remember / forget / regret + -ing = past action; stop + to-infinitive = stop in order to do

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: What a beautiful weather it is today!
The Himalayas stretch across several countries.
She is learning to play the sitar.
Honesty is a virtue that everyone admires.

steps: 'weather' is uncountable and cannot take 'a': 'What beautiful weather it is today!'.
The others are correct: 'the' with a mountain range and a musical instrument, and no article for 'Honesty' in a general sense.
solution.trap: 'What a beautiful day' is correct, which makes 'What a beautiful weather' sound right.
solution.rule: Articles: no 'a / an' with uncountable nouns (weather, advice, information, furniture)

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The house, which was built in 1920, is now a museum.
He is the man to whom I lent my bicycle.
The candidates, whom the panel thought were the best, were shortlisted.
This is the very book that I was looking for.

steps: The pronoun is the subject of 'were the best' ('the panel thought' is only inserted), so it must be 'who'.
The others are correct: 'which' in a non-defining clause, 'to whom' after a preposition, and 'that' after 'the very'.
solution.trap: 'the panel thought' sits between the pronoun and its verb and makes it look like an object.
solution.rule: who + inserted clause (I think, they said) + verb: the pronoun stays in the subject form

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Few of the guests stayed for dinner.
There were less mistakes in his second attempt.
Each of the rooms has an attached bathroom.
She drinks very little coffee these days.

steps: 'mistakes' is a countable plural, so it takes 'fewer': 'fewer mistakes'.
The others are correct: 'Few of the guests', 'Each of … has', and 'little coffee' (uncountable).
solution.trap: 'less' is so common in speech that 'less mistakes' sounds normal.
solution.rule: Quantifiers: fewer with countable plurals, less with uncountable nouns

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: She has been teaching here since 2018.
I will finish this report before you return.
He was reading when the lights went out.
We will go out as soon as the rain will stop.

steps: A time clause about the future ('as soon as …') takes the simple present: 'as soon as the rain stops'.
The others are correct: present perfect continuous with 'since', present tense after 'before', and past continuous interrupted by a past action.
solution.trap: 'will go' in the main clause pulls a second 'will' into the time clause.
solution.rule: No 'will' in time clauses (when, as soon as, before, after, until) about the future

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: She dare not to complain about the noise.
You needn't have brought a gift; your presence was enough.
He ought to have informed us earlier.
She didn't need to queue because she had booked online.

steps: 'dare not' works as a modal and takes the bare infinitive: 'She dare not complain'.
The others are correct: 'needn't have brought' (done but unnecessary), 'ought to have informed' (past duty not done) and 'didn't need to queue' (not necessary).
solution.trap: 'dare' can also be a main verb ('She does not dare to complain'), which makes 'to' look acceptable, but not after the modal 'dare not'.
solution.rule: Modal dare / need: dare not / need not + bare infinitive

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: This is the better of the two plans.
She is more intelligent than any other girl in her class.
His performance this year was inferior than last year's.

steps: 'inferior' takes 'to', not 'than': 'inferior to last year's'.
The others are correct: 'the better' of two, 'any other' within the same group, and a regular comparative.
solution.trap: 'last year's' correctly compares performance with performance, so the error is in the preposition.
solution.rule: Latin comparatives (inferior, superior, senior, junior, prior) + to

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Each of the students must bring his or her own pen.
The coach chose Ravi and he for the final.
Whom did you meet at the party?

steps: Ravi and the other person are the object of 'chose', so the object form is needed: 'Ravi and him'.
The others are correct: 'his or her' for 'Each', 'Whom' as the object of 'meet', and 'one … one's'.
solution.trap: Drop 'Ravi and': 'chose he' is clearly wrong.
solution.rule: Pronoun case: object form after a verb, even in a pair (Ravi and him)

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Had it not been for the scholarship, she could not have studied abroad.
If he were more careful, he would not have made so many mistakes in yesterday's test.
Should you change your mind, let us know by Friday.
If I had been informed earlier, I would have arranged a car.

steps: All four sentences are correct.

The first is an inverted third conditional; the second is a mixed conditional (a present trait, 'were more careful', with a past result); the third is an inverted first conditional with an instruction; the fourth is a passive third conditional.
solution.trap: The mixed conditional looks like a tense clash, but a present condition can explain a past result.
solution.rule: Conditionals: inverted forms (Had / Should) and mixed forms are correct when each clause matches its own time

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The quality of the products, not their price, determines our sales.
A good deal of the work has been done.
Two-thirds of the building was destroyed in the fire.
Each of the suggestions made by the members have been noted.

steps: The subject is 'Each', which is singular, so the verb must be 'has been noted'.
The others are correct: the subject is 'quality' ('not their price' is set aside), 'A good deal of' + uncountable takes a singular verb, and a fraction of a singular noun takes a singular verb.
solution.trap: Two plural nouns, 'suggestions' and 'members', come between 'Each' and the verb.
solution.rule: Agreement: each (of) → singular; fraction + singular noun → singular; 'not X' does not affect the verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The manager said that the bank will remain closed the following day.
He said that he had been ill since Monday.
She told me that she would be leaving the next morning.
I asked him whether he could lend me his notes.

steps: After the past 'said', and with 'the following day', 'will' must shift to 'would': 'the bank would remain closed'.
The others are correct back-shifts: 'had been', 'would be leaving' and 'could lend'.
solution.trap: Bank closures feel like a fixed fact, but this is a one-off announcement, not a universal truth.
solution.rule: Reported speech: will → would after a past reporting verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Rarely does one come across such courage.
So tired was she that she fell asleep at her desk.
Not a single word did he utter during the meeting.
On no account should the vault be left unlocked.

steps: All four sentences are correct.
Each begins with a negative or restrictive expression ('Rarely', 'So tired', 'Not a single word', 'On no account') and correctly puts the auxiliary before the subject.
solution.trap: Inverted word order looks unusual, which tempts you to mark one of them wrong.
solution.rule: Inversion after negative and restrictive expressions at the start of a sentence
